title: Recognising self-harm and suicidal ideation
blurb: Ask about suicide directly and kindly, focus on needs and immediate safety rather than risk scores, and build a safety plan with the person.
question: Liam, 22, attends the emergency department after cutting his arm. The local form asks the nurse to grade his suicide risk as low, medium or high to decide whether he needs a mental health assessment. What does NICE NG225 advise?

teach.body: Self-harm means intentional self-poisoning or self-injury, whatever the apparent purpose of the act. People who self-harm or have suicidal thoughts present everywhere: surgical wards, community visits, outpatient clinics. Proficiencies P3.10 and P4.11 ask every nurse to recognise and assess these signs and to start and evaluate interventions. In plain English: notice, ask directly and kindly, keep the person safe now, and connect them with the right help.
teach.cite: NMC Standards of proficiency (2018) P3.10, P4.11, Annexe B 1.1.6; NICE NG225 (2022)

teach.body: If someone seems hopeless, feels a burden or talks about not wanting to go on, ask clearly: "Are you having thoughts of ending your life?" A direct, calm question shows you can hear the answer and opens the way to help. Treat the person with respect, dignity and compassion, explore what the self-harm means for them, and remember each person self-harms for their own reasons, which may change from episode to episode.

teach.h: Scenario: Joanne on the orthopaedic ward
teach.body: Joanne, 41, is recovering from a fall. She has been tearful, says she feels 'a burden to everyone' and has stopped eating. Nurse Sam sits with her in a quiet room and asks directly whether she is having thoughts of suicide. She says she has. Sam asks whether she has any plans or means, stays with her, informs the nurse in charge and the medical team, and requests a liaison psychiatry assessment. She records Joanne's own words.

teach.text: Old habit, new rule: a low, medium or high risk grade must not decide who gets treatment or discharge (NG225 1.6). A 'low risk' label has never meant 'safe'. Also, harm minimisation and safety plans are collaborative: they are made WITH the person, not handed to them.

items: Ask directly and compassionately about thoughts of suicide.
No risk tools or low/medium/high grading to predict suicide or decide treatment or discharge (NG225 1.6).
First contact: severity, emotional state, immediate safety and means, safeguarding, then refer.
Don't delay psychosocial assessment for medical treatment or alcohol levels; assess safety before anyone leaves.
Safety plan: written with the person, held by them, shared as they decide (NG225 1.11.7-1.11.8).

summary: You can now recognise signs that a person may be at risk, ask about suicide directly, respond to self-harm in line with NICE NG225 without relying on risk scores, and help build a collaborative safety plan.

A.q: Joanne, 41, is on an orthopaedic ward after a fall. She has been tearful, says she feels 'a burden to everyone' and has stopped eating. What is the nurse's most appropriate action?
options: Refer her to the dietitian and monitor her food intake
Encourage her to focus on her recovery and her family
Ask her directly and compassionately about suicidal thoughts
Suggest she speaks to her GP about her low mood after discharge
A.why: Feeling a burden, tearfulness and withdrawal may indicate suicidal thinking (P3.10, Annexe B 1.1.6). Asking directly and compassionately allows the nurse to respond and escalate; NICE NG225 focuses on the person's needs and immediate safety.

whyNot.0: Nutrition matters, but this misses the emotional distress behind it.
whyNot.1: Encouragement without exploring her feelings may leave suicidal thoughts unrecognised.
whyNot.3: Deferring to after discharge leaves a possible current risk unassessed.

A.q: Liam, 22, attends the emergency department after cutting his arm. A local form asks the nurse to grade his suicide risk as low, medium or high. What does NICE NG225 advise?
options: Use the grade to decide whether he needs a mental health review
Complete it, then repeat it every four hours while he waits
Grade him as high risk to make sure he is seen more quickly
Do not use the grade to predict risk or to decide on discharge
A.why: NICE NG225 recs 1.6.1-1.6.4: do not use risk tools or global low, medium or high stratification to predict suicide or repetition, or to decide who is offered treatment or discharged.

whyNot.0: NG225 says scores must not determine who is offered treatment.
whyNot.1: Repeating a score does not make it a valid basis for decisions.
whyNot.2: Inflating a grade is inaccurate and still relies on stratification.

A.q: Mr Doyle, 55, tells his community mental health nurse he has been saving his prescribed tablets and has a large supply at home. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Discuss removing the tablets with him and agree a safety plan
Note the stockpile and review it at his next routine visit
Ask his GP to stop all of his medication with immediate effect
Tell him firmly that stockpiling medicines is dangerous
A.why: NICE NG225 rec 1.7.1: establish the means of self-harm and, if accessible, discuss removing them through therapeutic collaboration or negotiation to keep the person safe.

whyNot.1: Accessible means with this disclosure need action now, not at a later visit.
whyNot.2: Stopping all medication abruptly may cause harm and does not address his distress.
whyNot.3: A warning without collaboration does not reduce access or support him.

B.q: Ayesha, 19, attended the emergency department after an overdose. Before liaison psychiatry sees her, she says she wants to go home. What should happen first?
options: Let her go and ask her GP to follow her up within a week
Ask her to sign a self-discharge form and let her go
Ask security to prevent her leaving the department
Assess her safety and mental health before she leaves
B.why: NICE NG225 rec 1.5.14: if a person who has self-harmed wants to leave before a full psychosocial assessment, assess their safety and any mental health problems before they leave. Capacity and duty of care are considered too (rec 1.7.1).

whyNot.0: Letting her go without any safety assessment ignores NG225.
whyNot.1: A form does not replace an assessment of her safety.
whyNot.2: Restricting her without assessment is not justified; capacity and safety must be assessed first.

B.q: Ben, 34, is admitted to a medical ward after self-harm while intoxicated. He is now talking coherently. A doctor suggests waiting until his blood alcohol level is zero before referring him. What should the nurse advise?
options: Wait, so that the assessment is as accurate as possible
Wait until his medical treatment has been fully completed
Refer now, as alcohol levels should not delay assessment
Refer once he has signed consent for the assessment
B.why: NICE NG225 rec 1.5.4: do not use breath or blood alcohol levels to delay the psychosocial assessment. Rec 1.5.2: do not delay it until medical treatment is complete.

whyNot.0: NG225 specifically says alcohol levels should not be used to delay assessment.
whyNot.1: Physical and psychosocial care should happen concurrently (rec 1.7.3).
whyNot.3: Written consent is not a prerequisite for referral.

B.q: Before discharge, a nurse helps Sophie, 27, who self-harms, to develop a safety plan. Which description best follows NICE NG225?
options: Written with and agreed by Sophie, and held by her
Written by the team and filed in her hospital records
Written by her GP and sent to her family members
Written by Sophie herself and kept private from others
B.why: NICE NG225 recs 1.11.7-1.11.8: a safety plan is developed in partnership, uses a problem-solving approach, is held by the person and shared with family and professionals as she decides.

whyNot.1: A plan written for her and filed away is not collaborative or accessible in a crisis.
whyNot.2: Sharing with family is her decision, and the plan is made with her.
whyNot.3: It is developed collaboratively and shared as she decides, so it is accessible in a crisis.

C.q: A district nurse visits Mr Shaw, 68, whose wife died recently. He has given his dog to a neighbour and written letters to his children, and says he feels 'at peace now'. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Accept that he is coming to terms with his loss
Ask directly whether he is thinking of ending his life
Suggest a bereavement group and visit again next week
Phone his children to ask whether they share any concerns
C.why: Giving away possessions, putting affairs in order and sudden calm after a loss may signal suicidal intent (Annexe B 1.1.6, P3.10). A direct question allows the nurse to assess immediate safety and act (NICE NG225).

whyNot.0: Taking calm at face value may miss serious risk.
whyNot.2: Support may help later, but possible immediate risk needs assessing now.
whyNot.3: Contacting family without asking him first bypasses him and delays a direct assessment.

C.q: Kai, 17, is on a paediatric ward after self-harm. A student nurse asks what NICE NG225 says should happen while Kai is an inpatient. Which is correct?
options: A joint daily review by the paediatric and mental health teams
Mental health review after he is medically fit for discharge
Visits from family limited until his assessment is complete
A risk score repeated daily to decide on his level of observation
C.why: NICE NG225 rec 1.7.24: children and young people admitted after self-harm should have access to CYPMHS or liaison psychiatry 24 hours a day, a joint daily review by both teams, and daily access to family or carers.

whyNot.1: Assessment should not wait until medical treatment is complete.
whyNot.2: NG225 recommends daily access to family members or carers.
whyNot.3: Risk scores must not be used to drive decisions about care.

C.q: Ms Fenwick, 30, attends the emergency department for the fifth time this month after self-harm. A colleague says she should be warned she will be reported for 'misusing services'. What does NICE NG225 advise?
options: Warn her, as repeat attendances may delay care for others
Ask her GP to manage future episodes in the community
Treat her injuries and discharge her without referral
Arrange a multidisciplinary review to agree a joint plan
C.why: NICE NG225 rec 1.5.17: for frequent self-harm, carry out a multidisciplinary review with the person to agree a joint plan, including a safety plan. Rec 1.7.5: do not use punitive or criminal justice approaches for frequent self-harm.

whyNot.0: Punitive approaches for frequent self-harm are specifically not recommended (rec 1.7.5).
whyNot.1: Redirecting her elsewhere does not provide the joint plan NG225 recommends.
whyNot.2: Each attendance should include mental health input (rec 1.7.14).

reteach.title: Notice, ask, protect, connect
reteach.question: If you remember four verbs for any setting, what should they be?

blocks.body: NOTICE: tearfulness, hopelessness, feeling a burden, withdrawal, putting affairs in order. ASK: directly and kindly about thoughts of suicide or self-harm. PROTECT: treat injuries, check immediate safety, discuss removing accessible means together, consider safeguarding. CONNECT: refer for a psychosocial assessment and build a safety plan with the person. Don't let a risk score do the thinking.

blocks.text: A 'low risk' score is not reassurance. NICE says don't use scores to decide care.

explain.body: Signs may include tearfulness, hopelessness, feeling a burden, withdrawal or putting affairs in order. Ask directly and compassionately about suicidal thoughts; treat the person with respect and dignity.

test.q: Which question is most appropriate to ask a patient who says life feels pointless?
options: "Are you having thoughts of ending your life?"
"You're not thinking of doing anything silly, are you?"
"Have you told your family how you're feeling?"
"Would it help to talk to the chaplain today?"
test.why: A clear, direct, non-judgemental question about suicidal thoughts invites an honest answer.

whyNot.1: This leading, minimising question invites the answer 'no'.
whyNot.2: It moves away from assessing the person's own thoughts.
whyNot.3: Spiritual support may help, but it avoids asking about suicide.

explain.body: NICE NG225: do not use risk tools or low/medium/high stratification to predict suicide or repetition, or to decide treatment or discharge. Focus on needs and immediate and long-term safety; mental health professionals do a risk formulation.

test.q: What should a nurse's assessment after self-harm focus on, according to NICE NG225?
options: A validated suicide risk score
Predicting repetition of self-harm
Grading risk as low, medium or high
The person's needs and safety
test.why: NG225 rec 1.6.5: focus on the person's needs and how to support their immediate and long-term psychological and physical safety.

whyNot.0: Risk tools should not be used to predict suicide.
whyNot.1: Predicting repetition with tools is specifically not recommended.
whyNot.2: Global stratification should not be used to predict or decide care.

explain.body: Establish the means and, if accessible, discuss removing them collaboratively. Check severity of injury, emotional state, safeguarding and capacity. Don't delay psychosocial assessment for medical treatment or alcohol levels; assess safety before anyone leaves early.

test.q: A man who self-harmed tells the nurse he has a ligature at home. What does NG225 recommend?
options: Ask the police to search his home
Record it for the mental health team to raise
Discuss removing it with him collaboratively
Tell him he cannot go home while it is there
test.why: NG225 rec 1.7.1: establish the means and, if accessible, discuss removing them with therapeutic collaboration or negotiation.

whyNot.0: A police search is not the collaborative approach NG225 describes.
whyNot.1: Accessible means should be addressed now, not left for later.
whyNot.3: An ultimatum is not collaborative and may damage engagement.

explain.body: Made in partnership; identify triggers and warning signs, coping strategies, people and places for distraction, people to help, service and out-of-hours contacts, and ways to keep the environment safe. Held by the person; shared as they decide (NG225 1.11.7-1.11.8).

test.q: Who should hold a person's safety plan, according to NICE NG225?
options: The person's GP practice
The person themselves
The local crisis team
The person's next of kin
test.why: NG225 rec 1.11.8: the safety plan should be held by the person and shared with family, carers and professionals as the person decides.

whyNot.0: Professionals may have a copy, but the person holds the plan.
whyNot.2: The plan is the person's own and must be accessible to them in a crisis.
whyNot.3: Family may have a copy if the person decides, but it belongs to the person.
